title: Utility-scale quantum-repeater internet

concept.text: A utility-scale quantum-repeater internet would deliver entanglement between distant endpoints as a usable network service. Entanglement provides shared quantum correlations that applications can consume. In the memory-based architectures considered here, neighboring stations first establish elementary entangled links and receive a herald indicating successful preparation. Quantum memories hold successful links while others are prepared, and entanglement swapping connects those links into an entangled pair shared by the endpoints.

The innovation is the reliable operation of this process across multiple repeater stations, with distance, delivered-pair rate and entanglement quality sufficient for a specified application. The target service would avoid requiring trust in every intermediate station. An elementary memory link is an enabling component; achieving the proposed utility also requires coordinated swapping, memory management, error handling and network operation.

significance.text: If achieved, dependable long-distance entanglement would give separated users a shared quantum resource beyond ordinary classical communication. Its immediate significance would be the ability to supply certified entanglement and support suitable entanglement-based key-generation protocols across distant sites. The supplied repeater analysis explicitly models cryptographic use and identifies distributed quantum computing as a possible further application. These are conditional benefits of an operational network, not evidence that such a service has already been delivered.

Scientific distinction: device-independent cryptography would require more than delivery of entangled pairs or a reported Bell-inequality violation. A suitable security protocol, experimental conditions, detection performance and security analysis must also support usable secret-key generation. The supplied metropolitan Bell result does not establish those requirements, and the supplied theoretical key-rate calculation concerns BB84 rather than a demonstrated device-independent service.

Conditional synthesis: entanglement-based sensing and the connection of many fault-tolerant quantum processors could eventually extend the impact beyond communication security. Each would require additional application-specific capabilities; a functioning repeater network would not by itself establish useful distributed sensing or scalable distributed computation. The internet analogy concerns a shared network resource available to multiple applications. It does not imply that entanglement replaces classical communication or that every proposed quantum application becomes practical once connectivity exists.

The trust distinction matters. A trusted-node quantum-key-distribution backbone requires users to trust intermediate key handling; describing those stations as seeing decrypted quantum states misstates the issue. Such a backbone can provide a useful service, but it does not satisfy this proposal for end-to-end entanglement without trust in every intermediate site. The computer-engineering challenge is to turn quantum memories and optical links into a coordinated system through architecture, multiplexing, scheduling, error management and network operation, while relying substantially on advances in quantum optics and memory physics.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this proposal is sustained, application-useful end-to-end entanglement across a chain of repeater stations. Fiber transmission decreases exponentially with distance. Dividing the route into elementary links helps only if successful entanglement can be stored and connected before memory decay, operational errors and additional losses make the endpoint state unusable. A fast elementary link therefore does not by itself establish a fast or high-quality multi-link network.

Concrete barriers include memory coherence, efficient preparation and retrieval, reliable two-qubit operations and measurements, sufficient trial rates, and coordinating probabilistic link successes. Multiplexing provides more opportunities to prepare entanglement, but the network must still select, store and connect successful events. The metropolitan experiment's scalability discussion identifies Bell-state measurements on time-bin entangled states with arbitrary delays as a further requirement for swapping between elementary links.

The Kinos and colleagues model identifies memory coherence of roughly one second and two-qubit gate and measurement errors around 10⁻³ as important targets for its analyzed long-distance repeater scheme. Those figures are architecture-dependent targets alongside efficiencies, trial rates and other assumptions. They are neither universal sufficient conditions nor measured specifications of an operating network.

Engineering synthesis: a utility must also manage the joint trade-off among distance, fidelity, throughput and availability. Scheduling must accommodate unequal link waiting times; error management must preserve application-level quality through successive connections; and operation must remain stable despite calibration needs and equipment interruptions. The reported cryogenic memories also make cooling and supporting infrastructure relevant to practical deployment. These system requirements remain distinct from demonstrating any single favorable laboratory parameter.

current_state.text: The April 2026 version of the Zhu and colleagues preprint described in the supplied review reports a metropolitan elementary link between solid-state quantum memories separated by 14.5 km, connected through 17.8 km of deployed fiber. It reports a CHSH parameter of S = 2.22 ± 0.06, described as a 3.7-standard-deviation violation. This is evidence for reported Bell nonlocality at that link's operating point. It does not demonstrate a connected chain of elementary repeater links, an application-ready multi-hop service or loophole-free device-independent key generation.

At the Bell-test-quality operating point, the reported entanglement distribution rate is 5.5 ± 0.2 mHz, with fidelity of 78.6% ± 2.0%. The research associates this point with 3 mW pump power and a 20 ns acceptance window. The maximum reported rate is 0.94 ± 0.01 Hz; the reviewed supplementary comparison gives fidelity F = 0.606 ± 0.007 at that higher-rate point. The research associates the higher rate with 18 mW pump power and a 40 ns window. The near-hertz rate must therefore not be combined with the higher-fidelity Bell-test result as though they occurred together.

The research further reports operation near 3 K and multiplexing across 1,205 temporal modes, providing useful context for the hardware and the elementary-link rate. The retained PDF extraction skipped some form content after reaching an extraction limit. According to the supplied review, the relevant rate, fidelity and Bell-result values remained available in prose and table text. This partial extraction does not invalidate those reported values, but it limits claims about comprehensive inspection of the document.

The supplied research lists the Zhu work as a Nature Photonics publication dated 7 May 2026, volume 20, pages 812–817. The supplied review grounds its findings in the retained preprint, so those final journal bibliographic details remain unverified here. The experimental account above is attributed to the preprint rather than treating the research's journal citation as independently confirmed.

The retained author preprint by Adam Kinos, Andreas Walther, Stefan Kröll and Lars Rippe, titled Complete analysis of a realistic fiber-based quantum repeater scheme, is dated 25 April 2025, following a revision on 24 April. It calculates secret-key rates spanning 1 to 1000 Hz at 1000 km across modeled parameter choices. Roughly one-second memory coherence and gate and measurement errors around 10⁻³ are important targets within that analysis, together with other efficiency and trial-rate assumptions. The modeled application is BB84 key generation. These are calculated possibilities, not measurements of a 1000 km network.

The supplied APS citation was represented in the retained evidence by an alternative author preprint. That copy verifies the work's title, authors and modeled results, but not the claimed final publication date of 28 August 2025, Physical Review Research volume 7 article 033199, or the assertion that a published PDF header prints DOI 10.1103/frtv-p5zy. This version limitation leaves those publication details unresolved; it is not evidence that the theoretical result is false.

The research identifies the 2023 Azuma and colleagues review, Quantum repeaters: From quantum networks to the quantum internet, as an architectural survey, and the 2018 Wehner, Elkouss and Hanson article, Quantum internet: A vision for the road ahead, as a staged vision. Neither has a retained artifact in the supplied source index. The research reports only a visible journal-page summary for the Science article and no accessible full text. These references provide bibliographic context here, rather than independently reviewed support for detailed architectural or application claims.

Evidence boundary: the supplied materials establish an elementary-link experiment and a theoretical route toward longer networks. The freshness record is empty, so they do not establish the worldwide experimental frontier as of 1 November 2026. The proposal is not demonstrated by these inputs, but those inputs also cannot establish that no later or other experiment has met comparable milestones.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed engineering milestone: deliver end-to-end entanglement through at least two intermediate repeater stations over hundreds of kilometers, at a sustained delivered-pair rate of at least 1 Hz. Certify the required entanglement quality at the same operating point used to measure that rate. These distance, station-count and throughput thresholds are proposed criteria for this record, not established scientific standards.
completion_criteria.label: Quality-certified 1-Hz entanglement through two repeaters over hundreds of kilometers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional demonstration: use the delivered entanglement for a specified application, such as device-independent key distribution with its security requirements satisfied, or verified entanglement connection between independently operated networks. State the Bell-test assumptions, event-selection rules, accepted-pair definition, averaging interval and application-level performance. A Bell violation alone would not demonstrate a secure-key service, and a headline generation rate would not establish usable application throughput.
completion_criteria.label: Specified application of delivered entanglement with stated conditions and performance

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: repeat the demonstration across multiple operating sessions, disclose calibration and downtime, provide enough protocol and analysis detail for independent assessment, and seek reproduction by an independent team or on an independently configured network. Report distance, quality, throughput and availability together, including their uncertainties and any postselection. Repeated finite tests would establish demonstrated operating breadth and reliability within stated conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated sessions with joint operating disclosures and sought independent reproduction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: document the supported topology, number of users, memory and cooling requirements, classical coordination, trust assumptions, operating resources and failure recovery. Show that elementary links are actually connected into endpoint entanglement. A single 14.5 km memory link or a trusted-node key backbone would not meet this milestone. Meeting it would establish a bounded multi-repeater capability, not universal interoperability, commercial economics or the ability to connect arbitrary quantum processors.
completion_criteria.label: Elementary links connected into endpoint entanglement with documented practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CPE-01, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer, concerns reliable computation within a quantum processing system; CPE-07 concerns distributing entanglement between sites. They overlap when networking quantum processors, an application direction supported by the repeater analysis. The supplied roster contains only CPE-01's title, so it does not establish a precise dependency. Useful quantum networking should not be made categorically dependent on achieving the full CPE-01 milestone.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-04, Cascadable general-purpose photonic computer with optical memory, overlaps through optical components, memory interfaces and the challenge of preserving useful signals through successive operations. Its target is general-purpose computation with photonic machinery; CPE-07 uses photons and memories to distribute quantum entanglement. Achieving one would not by itself establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-03, General-purpose fabric that retires data-movement dominance, shares an interest in communication architecture and the cost of moving information. Its stated target concerns data movement in computing systems. CPE-07 instead concerns preparing, storing and connecting entanglement under quantum loss and error constraints. The shared systems concerns do not make them the same innovation.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-06, Wall-plug-superior superconducting classical computer at useful scale, has a practical connection through cryogenic infrastructure and accounting for supporting energy costs. The supplied quantum-memory experiment operates near 3 K, but that does not make it a superconducting classical computer or establish favorable wall-plug economics. The concepts target different functions and performance criteria.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-02, Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer; CPE-05, Mammalian-scale neuromorphic learning machine near biological energy; and CPE-08, Economically manufacturable atomic-density defect-tolerant digital computer, address distinct computational, energy or manufacturing breakthroughs. Their titles supply no specific technical dependency on quantum repeaters. General concerns such as efficiency, reliability and scale are insufficient grounds to merge any of these entries with CPE-07.

change_log.reason: The sources do not establish that all repeater architectures use this design or that all current experiments are single elementary links.

change_log.reason: The figures are useful architectural projections, not measured network performance or universal sufficient conditions.

change_log.change: Clarified the proposed milestone as two intermediate repeater stations and required simultaneous rate and quality certification, application evidence and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: This resolves hop ambiguity and makes the proposed demonstration assessable without presenting its thresholds as consensus standards.

unresolved_issues: The worldwide experimental frontier as of 1 November 2026 remains unestablished because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The final publication details and version differences for the Zhu and Kinos works remain unverified through the supplied review; the claimed Kinos published-PDF DOI header is also unverified.
The Zhu PDF extraction skipped some form content. The review supports the reported central values, but comprehensive extraction of the document was not achieved.
The Azuma review and Science vision article have no retained artifacts. Detailed claims about their contents cannot be independently resolved from these inputs.

The proposed application must still determine its required entanglement quality, security assumptions, acceptable availability and resource economics. A 1 Hz pair rate alone does not answer those questions.
Exact dependencies on other roster concepts and the assertion that CPE-07 was absent from the historical ten cannot be verified without their fuller records and the historical list.

brief.title: A dependable long-distance quantum network
possible: People at distant sites could share entanglement: quantum correlations they can use to generate secret keys. A dependable network would deliver this resource through intermediate stations without requiring users to trust every station.
why: This would give separated users a shared quantum resource beyond ordinary communication. It would support secure communication across distant sites and provide a foundation for connecting quantum computers.

sources.showed: In a preprint, the team reported entanglement between quantum memories, devices that store quantum states, separated by 14.5 km. A Bell test found correlations beyond the limits of classical physics.
sources.quote:
We observe a CHSH-Bell inequality violation
by 3.7 standard deviations, marking the first certification of Bell nonlocality in metropolitan-scale
quantum repeaters.
sources.cited_for: The experiment demonstrates a building block for a longer network.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate a chain of connected memory links or a usable secure-key service.

sources.showed: This is a survey of quantum repeater architectures, which connect shorter quantum links into longer ones.
sources.cited_for: It provides architectural context for quantum repeater networks.
sources.not_established: An architectural survey does not demonstrate an operating network service.

sources.who: Stephanie Wehner, David Elkouss and Ronald Hanson
sources.showed: This is a staged vision for developing a quantum internet.
sources.cited_for: It provides context for developing quantum networks in stages.
sources.not_established: A proposed development path does not establish dependable long-distance operation.

sources.who: Adam Kinos, Andreas Walther, Stefan Kröll and Lars Rippe
sources.showed: Their theoretical analysis calculates secret-key generation across 1000 km under modeled hardware conditions. Reusing light emitters allows more frequent attempts to establish links.
sources.quote:
This time multiplexing increases the protocol trial rate by up to
an order of magnitude.
sources.cited_for: The model identifies hardware targets and a possible route to long-distance key generation.
sources.not_established: Calculated performance is not a measurement of an operating long-distance network.

shown: Zhu and colleagues demonstrated a city-scale memory link with correlations confirmed by a Bell test. Their fastest operation approached a pair per second, but the stronger correlations required slower operation. Neither result demonstrates delivery through a chain of repeater stations.
missing: A chain must store and connect successful links before stored quantum states decay or accumulated errors make them unusable.
Delivered entanglement must support a specified application with useful speed and quality under the same operating conditions.
A network must sustain service through unequal link waiting times, calibration, equipment interruptions and recovery.

milestones.label: Certified entanglement delivered steadily across a long chain
milestones.explanation: A network would have to deliver at least a pair each second through two or more intermediate stations over hundreds of kilometers, certifying quality under those conditions. This would establish sustained delivery across a chain.

milestones.label: Delivered entanglement supports a specified application
milestones.explanation: An application would have to work with stated assumptions, event-selection rules, accepted-pair definitions, averaging periods and measured performance. This would establish usable output beyond a Bell-test result.

milestones.label: Repeated operation supports independent assessment and reproduction
milestones.explanation: Repeated sessions would have to report distance, quality, speed, availability, uncertainty, calibration, downtime and event selection, with independent reproduction sought. This would establish reliability under stated conditions.

milestones.label: Connected endpoints work within documented practical limits
milestones.explanation: Connected links would have to deliver endpoint entanglement with network layout, user capacity, memory, cooling, coordination, trust, resources and recovery documented. This would establish a capability with clear operating limits.

uncertain: The required entanglement quality, security assumptions and acceptable availability depend on the application.
A Bell-test violation alone does not establish secure-key generation without trusting the devices.
The resources and operating costs needed for a useful service remain open questions.

page.title: Continental quantum-repeater networks
page.definition: A chain of quantum repeaters distributes entanglement across continental distances over optical fibre. In a memory-based repeater, quantum memories hold states on adjacent links until a joint measurement at the repeater entangles the outer qubits. Repeating this operation extends the shared state to the endpoints. Classical signals coordinate the links, and quantum error correction addresses photon loss and errors in local operations. Trusted key relays instead pass classical key material between successive stations.

goal.need: At 1550 nm, only about one photon in 100 survives 100 km of standard single-mode fibre. An ordinary amplifier cannot copy an unknown quantum state. China’s quantum key network reaches 80 cities by relying on trusted relays. With end-to-end entanglement, distant users could establish encryption keys without entrusting them to those relays. Quantum processors at different sites could also perform gates between their qubits. Each use requires entangled pairs of sufficient fidelity.

statements.quote: Interstate Quantum Entanglement Distribution using Quantum Repeaters
statements.context: Milestone 4 of the Quantum Internet Blueprint Workshop report specifies continental distances and correction of loss and operational errors.

statements.quote: fully functional quantum repeaters unlocking Pan-European end-to-end quantum communication.

completion.title: Concatenated quantum repeaters distribute entanglement across continental distances with error correction.
completion.criterion: Demonstrate interstate entanglement distribution over continental distances through concatenated quantum repeaters, with quantum communication corrected for loss and operational errors and integrated classical and quantum networking.
completion.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Report of the DOE Quantum Internet Blueprint Workshop (2020), section 3.4, Milestone 4.
completion.threshold_quote: quantum repeaters and quantum error corrected communication with respect to loss and operational errors over continental-scale distances
completion.basis: DOE places this demonstration after the intercity quantum-memory network and gives no fixed distance in kilometres or minimum service rate. Kinos and colleagues calculated secret-key rates of 1–1000 Hz at 1000 km across modelled parameter sets. The completion test requires an experimental network.

milestones.title: Two quantum memories share entanglement heralded independently of endpoint measurement.
milestones.criterion: Generate entanglement between two separated quantum memories. Signal success with an event independent of measuring the two stored qubits, so the memories still hold the entangled state when success is announced.
milestones.set_by: Community convention for heralding, defined in Wehner, Elkouss and Hanson's 2018 staged vision; applied to memory-based elementary links.
milestones.threshold_quote: signal the successful generation of entanglement by an event that is independent of the (immediate) measurement of the entangled qubits themselves.

milestones.title: Two remote memories deliver states with average Bell-state fidelity above 0.5 at preset times.
milestones.criterion: Deliver a two-qubit state at every preset time, including cycles in which all entangling attempts failed. The fidelity, or overlap with the target Bell state, must exceed 0.5 on average over all delivered states, without preselection or postselection.
milestones.set_by: Humphreys et al., Figure 1a's deterministic-delivery benchmark; QuTech identifies the 2018 on-demand demonstration as a quantum-internet milestone.
milestones.threshold_quote: Deterministic entanglement delivery guarantees the output of states with average entanglement fidelity exceeding 0.5 at pre-specified times.

milestones.title: A memory node swaps two stored links into heralded entanglement between nonadjacent endpoints.
milestones.criterion: Establish entanglement on two links that meet at a memory node, storing the first link while generating the second. Perform a joint Bell-state measurement at the middle node and use its outcome to apply the endpoint correction. Herald entanglement between the two outer nodes independently of measuring their qubits.
milestones.set_by: Community convention for swapping stored remote entanglement, identified in Azuma et al. (2023), Section V.H.3, and demonstrated by Pompili et al. (2021).
milestones.threshold_quote: deterministic entanglement swapping in a heralded fashion between distant nodes that were not originally connected.

milestones.title: Memory-assisted communication exceeds the repeaterless secret-key capacity per channel use.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a memory-assisted secret-key rate greater than −log₂(1−η) secret bits per optical mode, where η is the end-to-end transmissivity of the comparison pure-loss channel. Use the same end-to-end loss and a consistent count of optical modes for the protocol and the direct-transmission bound.
milestones.set_by: Pirandola, Laurenza, Ottaviani and Banchi's 2017 capacity theorem; Azuma et al., Section IV, recognises exceeding repeaterless bounds as a repeater-development milestone.
milestones.threshold_quote: the repeaterless bound K(η) = − log2(1 − η)

milestones.title: An intercity memory network stores entanglement and teleports qubits between any two end nodes.
milestones.criterion: Connect cities by entanglement swapping so any two end nodes can obtain and store entangled quantum bits and teleport quantum information between them. End nodes support local measurements and operations; storage accommodates round-trip classical communication. DOE sets no fixed kilometre or storage-time threshold.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Quantum Internet Blueprint (2020), Milestone 3, official summary.
milestones.threshold_quote: INTERCITY QUANTUM COMMUNICATION USING ENTANGLEMENT SWAPPING.

milestones.title: A quantum repeater node performs quantum error correction.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate quantum error correction on encoded quantum information at a repeater node. The roadmap gives no numerical logical-error-rate threshold for this node-level demonstration.
milestones.set_by: Fraunhofer ISI, German Umbrella Project for Quantum Communication (SquAD), Quantum Repeaters – A Technology Roadmap, Figure 7.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate error correction at repeater node

milestones.title: Any two users on an inter-campus or intra-city network can obtain and measure entangled qubits.
milestones.criterion: Distribute end-to-end entanglement between any chosen pair of users on an inter-campus or intra-city network. Generate the entanglement deterministically or herald success independently of the users’ measurements. Both users must be able to measure their qubits locally.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Quantum Internet Blueprint (2020), Milestone 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: end-to-end creation of quantum entanglement in a deterministic or heralded fashion, as well as local measurements.

milestones.title: Two metropolitan-scale networks share entanglement through a repeater backbone longer than 500 km.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate an integrated prototype that distributes entanglement between two metropolitan-scale networks through quantum repeaters on a standard optical-fibre backbone longer than 500 km. The distance applies to the backbone.
milestones.set_by: Quantum Internet Alliance, Horizon Europe Phase 1 grant agreement 101102140 (2022), prototype network objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: two metropolitan-scale networks via a long-distance backbone (>500 km) using quantum repeaters.

not_found: No universal service-level pair-rate, fidelity or availability threshold was found in the DOE roadmaps, RFC 9340 or the cited reviews.
No experimental report satisfying the complete DOE intercity memory-network test or continental concatenated-repeater target was found.

results.finding: Two remote solid-state memories yielded 78.6 ± 2.0% Bell-state fidelity across 712 fourfold coincidences.
results.detail: The 712 events are summed across the three measurement bases in Table S5. The fidelity was measured at 3 mW with a 20-ns coincidence window.
results.quote:
At a pump power of 3 mW
and a 20-ns coincidence window, entanglement-witness
measurements on the retrieved atomic excitation yield a
fidelity of 78.6 ± 2.0% for |ψ+⟩ (Fig. 3b).

results.finding: The two memories yielded 78.6 ± 2.0% Bell-state fidelity across 712 selected fourfold coincidences.
results.detail: The analysis selected heralds with a 500-ns separation and required a retrieved photon detection at each endpoint. The reported fidelity excludes failed cycles.

results.finding: Central photonic swapping with endpoint feed-forward yielded 78.6 ± 2.0% fidelity across 712 fourfold coincidences.
results.detail: The memories were at the endpoints. The central station measured incoming photons to establish a single elementary repeater link.
results.quote:
When the two detections at node C originate from differ-
ent detectors, a signal prompts node A to apply a π phase
shift via the EOM, mapping the heralded state from |ψ−⟩
to |ψ+⟩, ensuring the delivered state is consistently |ψ+⟩.

results.finding: One intra-city user pair locally measured entanglement with a CHSH value of 2.22 ± 0.06.
results.detail: The central station supplied a herald and had no user qubit. The CHSH analysis required a detection at each of the two user endpoints.
results.quote:
As shown in Fig. 4, we observe a maximal vio-
lation of S = 2.22±0.06 exceeding the classical bound by
3.7 standard deviations.

results.finding: For two remote memory qubits, the modeled heralding probability per trial is η²/2.
results.detail: The model assumes negligible or measurable fibre phase shifts, indistinguishable photons and negligible detector dark counts.
results.quote:
Thus, the success probability for a HEG trial is
pHEG = η2/2, (4)

results.finding: The authors estimate remote Bell-pair fidelity conditional on success using 1,000 simulated sessions per setting.
results.detail: A session fails if any link has no successful entangling trial. Failed end-node purification also produces no final pair.
results.quote:
To validate the theoretical calculations, we also per-
form numerical simulations to estimate the rate and av-
erage fidelity of the final EPR pairs.

results.finding: Stored-link swapping into remote Bell pairs was modeled and checked over 1,000 simulated sessions per setting.
results.detail: The protocol records the endpoint Pauli frame and allows the corresponding correction to be applied using the middle-node outcomes.
results.quote:
After this, entanglement swapping combines the den-
sity matrices for all links, two at a time. This generates
a final density matrix for the EPR pair of that session.

results.finding: For one modeled 1,000 km rare-earth-ion repeater chain, the estimated secret-key rate is about 10 bits/s.
results.detail: The model uses 40% fibre-independent efficiency, 500 ms spin coherence and 0.001 initialization, gate and measurement error probabilities.
results.quote:
All combined, an experimental implementation of the
quantum repeater network spanning 1000 km should be
able to reach secret key rates of around 10 Hz as shown
in Fig. 5(a).

results.finding: Two atomic-ensemble memories showed heralded entanglement over 420 km of fibre.
results.detail: The 420 km is the total optical path, including long fibre spools. Both memories were at USTC, and the middle station was at Hefei Software Park.
results.quote:
In summary, we have experimentally realized entan-
glement between two quantum memories via fibers up
to 420 km.

results.finding: For two memories across six fibre-length settings, heralded entanglement probability per trial exceeded the plotted PLOB bound below a transmissivity of 10⁻⁴·⁵.
results.quote:
As shown in
Fig. 4, when channel transmittance is lower than10−4.5
(which refers to a distance over 230 km in our experi-
ment), the entangling probability in our experiment is
higher than the PLOB bound.

results.finding: Two trapped-ion memories shared heralded entanglement over 10 km of spooled fibre.
results.detail: The heralding mechanism is inferred from the abstract’s description of the single-photon entanglement protocol.
results.quote: Here we demonstrate memory–memory entanglement between two nodes connected by 10 km of spooled fibre surviving beyond the average entanglement establishment time.

results.finding: A two-node trapped-ion system yielded a positive asymptotic device-independent key rate over 101 km.
results.quote: we report a proof-of-principle device-independent quantum key distribution demonstration with finite-size analysis over 10 km and a positive key rate over 101 km in the asymptotic limit

results.finding: Two remote diamond spin qubits shared heralded entanglement with Bell-state fidelity 0.534.
results.detail: A detector-dependent phase flip delivered the same target Bell state for either detector click. The supplied text does not state the total number of heralded events.

results.finding: Two remote spin memories delivered states with Bell-state fidelity 0.534 on successful heralds.
results.detail: Delivery was triggered by the herald. The supplied text does not state the total number of heralded events.

results.finding: One pair of metropolitan-scale endpoints shared heralded entanglement over 25 km of deployed fiber and measured their qubits locally.
results.detail: The extensible architecture was demonstrated with two endpoint nodes and one midpoint heralding station.

results.finding: Two rubidium-ensemble memories 12.5 km apart shared independently heralded entanglement.
results.detail: The 107 μs storage run kept the state available after heralding. In the 5 μs delayed-choice run, endpoint readout preceded heralding.
results.quote: We demonstrated heralded entanglement generation between two quantum nodes situated 12.5 km apart, and the storage of entanglement exceeding the round-trip communication time.

results.finding: Two remote memories yielded a postselected Bell-state fidelity of 0.672(32) for the positive-sign state.
results.detail: The fidelity was measured on polarization states formed from the memory readouts and local probe pulses, with a detector click required at each endpoint.
results.quote:

results.finding: The Hefei network demonstrated heralded entanglement with local readout on all 3 user pairs.
results.detail: The all-pairs measurements used delayed-choice readout. Pair selection was randomized to simulate user requests.
results.quote: We also showed the concurrent entanglement generation on three links.

results.finding: Two remote diamond spin memories shared heralded entanglement with Bell-state fidelity 0.81(2).
results.detail: The source gives the number of memories but does not state the number of heralded events used for this fidelity estimate.
results.quote:
Choosing α to maximise ﬁdelity, we ﬁnd that our pro-
tocol allows us to generate entanglement with a ﬁdelity
of 0.81(2) at a rate ofrent = 6 Hz (forα = 0.05).

results.finding: Two remote diamond spin memories achieved mean Bell-state fidelity 0.56(1) in a 42,000-cycle experiment spanning multiple settings.
results.detail: Each run contained 1,500 cycles. The source gives the total across settings and does not specify the cycle count for the 9.9 Hz, α = 0.2 result. When no herald arrived, the spins were still delivered and read out.
results.quote:
We ﬁnd that forα = 0.2
and a rate of 9.9 Hz, we are able to create states with
a ﬁdelity of0.56(1), proving successful deterministic en-
tanglement delivery.

results.finding: Alice and Charlie’s stored NV-spin Bell states had fidelity 0.551(13) across 4,055 heralded events.
results.detail: The endpoint memories were the NV communication spins. Bob used a separate carbon-13 nuclear spin to store the first link.
results.quote:
Figure 5C compares the state ﬁdelities across the dif-
ferent BSM outcomes, displaying the expected lower ﬁ-
delities for outcomes of |1⟩ and an average ﬁdelity over
all outcomes of F = 0 .551(13).

results.finding: Alice–Charlie Bell-state fidelity averaged 0.551(13) across 4,055 heralded deliveries.
results.detail: The preset timeout triggered a restart. The reported average covers all Bell-measurement outcomes within heralded events.
results.quote:
Figure 5C compares the state ﬁdelities across the dif-
ferent BSM outcomes, displaying the expected lower ﬁ-
delities for outcomes of |1⟩ and an average ﬁdelity over
all outcomes of F = 0 .551(13).

results.finding: Bob’s memory-assisted swap produced Alice–Charlie Bell states with fidelity 0.551(13) across 4,055 heralded events.
results.detail: The herald required Bob to pass a charge-and-resonance check after the Bell-state measurement. The reported average includes all four Bell-measurement outcomes.
results.quote:
Figure 5C compares the state ﬁdelities across the dif-
ferent BSM outcomes, displaying the expected lower ﬁ-
delities for outcomes of |1⟩ and an average ﬁdelity over
all outcomes of F = 0 .551(13).

results.finding: Any pair in the three-node lab network could share entanglement. The swapped pair had fidelity 0.551(13) over 4,055 heralds.
results.quote:
We achieved multipar-
tite entanglement distribution across the three nodes and
any-to-any connectivity through entanglement swapping.

results.finding: Bob teleported his stored qubit to Charlie in 4,055 heralded swaps, giving Alice–Charlie Bell fidelity 0.551(13).
results.detail: The teleported qubit was Bob’s half of the Alice–Bob entangled state. The protocol used real-time classical feed-forward to Charlie.
results.quote:
One way to read
this protocol is that the BSM induces teleportation of
the state stored on Bob’s memory qubit to Charlie, by
consuming the entangled state shared by Bob’s commu-
nication qubit and Charlie.

results.finding: Across three nodes, heralded Alice–Charlie entanglement with storage at Charlie had an estimated Bell-state fidelity of 0.61.
results.detail: The adjacent-link heralds entangled electronic communication qubits. The final Alice–Charlie state was transferred to a dedicated memory qubit only at Charlie.
results.quote: At this point, the teleporter is ready and Alice and Charlie share an entangled state with an estimated fidelity of 0.61.

results.finding: Three-node entanglement swapping heralded an Alice–Charlie state with an estimated Bell-state fidelity of 0.61.
results.detail: The swap herald required an accepted Bob communication-qubit readout, consistent memory readouts and a passed charge-resonance check. The Bell-state fidelity was estimated.
results.quote: At this point, the teleporter is ready and Alice and Charlie share an entangled state with an estimated fidelity of 0.61.

results.finding: Charlie-to-Alice teleportation of six cardinal input states achieved mean fidelity 0.688(10) after heralded preparation.
results.detail: The teleportation step accepted every input after the shared entangled state had been prepared. This result used 7.5 ns optical detection windows.
results.quote:

results.finding: Two silicon-29 nuclear-spin memories shared photon-heralded entanglement over up to 40 km of spooled telecom fibre.
results.quote: Using this frequency conversion scheme together with the entanglement method described above (Fig.  3a ), we remotely entangle two  29 Si nuclei through spools of low-loss telecom fibre up to 40 km in length (Fig.  4b ).

results.finding: Two remote nuclear-spin memories achieved 0.64 ± 0.05 Bell-state fidelity on heralded trials before flag filtering.
results.detail: The raw fidelity still conditions on photon heralding. The 10 ms interval is a storage interval following entanglement generation.

results.finding: Electron-spin error flags at two memory nodes yielded nuclear Bell-state fidelity of 0.77 ± 0.05 after flagged trials were discarded.
results.detail: The protocol removed flagged trials from the fidelity estimate. It applied no recovery operation to the flagged nuclear states.
results.quote: After using error detection by discarding measurements in which the electronic flag qubits are measured in the |↑ e ⟩ state, the Bell-state fidelity is  F Φ nn −  ED = 0.77 ( 5 ) , which is an improvement from the directly measured value of  F Φ nn −  raw = 0.64 ( 5 )  without error detection.

results.finding: Two fixed memory nodes shared heralded entanglement over a 35 km deployed Boston-area fibre loop.
results.detail: The two laboratory endpoints were 6 m apart in line of sight. The fibre ran to an off-site location and back.
results.quote: We demonstrate that our system is compatible with conventional fibre infrastructure and is resilient to these error sources by generating nuclear entanglement through a 35-km loop of telecom fibre deployed in the Boston area urban environment (Fig.  4d ).

results.finding: Two rubidium quantum memory arrays generated independently heralded spin-wave entanglement at 1.6 kHz.
results.detail: The 1.6 kHz rate refers to the stored spin-wave states. The reported 546 Hz rate refers to the polarization-entangled state produced by fusing two such states during readout.
results.quote: The returned TTL signal heralds the successful generation of a memory-memory EME state, and the control units identify the specific pair of entangled memory cells based on the arrival time of the heralding signals.

results.finding: A diamond NV repeater-node prototype improved encoded spin–photon joint-state population with active bit-flip correction over up to 12 rounds (20,000 runs per setting).

definition = "A chain of quantum repeaters distributes entanglement across continental distances over optical fibre. In a memory-based repeater, quantum memories hold states on adjacent links until a joint measurement at the repeater entangles the outer qubits. Repeating this operation extends the shared state to the endpoints. Classical signals coordinate the links, and quantum error correction addresses photon loss and errors in local operations. Trusted key relays instead pass classical key material between successive stations.". Reason: The definition now explains what a swap does and distinguishes end-to-end entanglement from continental key delivery through trusted relays.

goal.need = "At 1550 nm, only about one photon in 100 survives 100 km of standard single-mode fibre. An ordinary amplifier cannot copy an unknown quantum state. China\u2019s quantum key network reaches 80 cities by relying on trusted relays. With end-to-end entanglement, distant users could establish encryption keys without entrusting them to those relays. Quantum processors at different sites could also perform gates between their qubits. Each use requires entangled pairs of sufficient fidelity.". Reason: The existing account quantifies fibre loss but omits the users who already depend on trusted relays and the condition for using shared entanglement.

add statement by U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, 2020: "Interstate Quantum Entanglement Distribution using Quantum Repeaters". Reason: The 2020 workshop report supplies the original date and names the network capability in its milestone heading.

add statement by Quantum Internet Alliance, Horizon Europe, 2022: "fully functional quantum repeaters unlocking Pan-European end-to-end quantum communication.". Reason: The European programme independently names a fibre repeater backbone as the route to pan-European end-to-end communication.

edit completion: set_by = "U.S. Department of Energy, Report of the DOE Quantum Internet Blueprint Workshop (2020), section 3.4, Milestone 4."; basis = "DOE places this demonstration after the intercity quantum-memory network and gives no fixed distance in kilometres or minimum service rate. Kinos and colleagues calculated secret-key rates of 1\u20131000 Hz at 1000 km across modelled parameter sets. The completion test requires an experimental network."; refs = [24, 4, 5]. Reason: Section 3.4 of the full workshop report confirms the existing test and clarifies that the published 1000 km calculation supplies no distance cutoff.

edit m1: criterion = "Generate entanglement between two separated quantum memories. Signal success with an event independent of measuring the two stored qubits, so the memories still hold the entangled state when success is announced."; refs = [6, 25, 7]. Reason: The current criterion mixes the heralding test with one experiment’s pump power, acquisition time and measured performance.

edit m2: criterion = "Deliver a two-qubit state at every preset time, including cycles in which all entangling attempts failed. The fidelity, or overlap with the target Bell state, must exceed 0.5 on average over all delivered states, without preselection or postselection.". Reason: The revision removes one apparatus’s distance, delivery rate and measured fidelity while preserving the all-cycle average that defines the test.

edit m3: criterion = "Establish entanglement on two links that meet at a memory node, storing the first link while generating the second. Perform a joint Bell-state measurement at the middle node and use its outcome to apply the endpoint correction. Herald entanglement between the two outer nodes independently of measuring their qubits.". Reason: The existing criterion appends a particular swapped-state fidelity and heralding rate to the test for joining two stored links.

edit m4: criterion = "Demonstrate a memory-assisted secret-key rate greater than \u2212log\u2082(1\u2212\u03b7) secret bits per optical mode, where \u03b7 is the end-to-end transmissivity of the comparison pure-loss channel. Use the same end-to-end loss and a consistent count of optical modes for the protocol and the direct-transmission bound."; threshold_quote = "the repeaterless bound K(\u03b7) = \u2212 log2(1 \u2212 \u03b7)"; threshold_ref = 11. Reason: The revision states the capacity comparison in secret bits per optical mode and removes the confidence level and security assumptions of one experiment.

add milestone after m3: "A quantum repeater node performs quantum error correction.". Reason: The completion test requires error-corrected communication, but the existing milestones do not test error correction at even one repeater.

add milestone after m4: "Any two users on an inter-campus or intra-city network can obtain and measure entangled qubits.". Reason: DOE distinguishes metropolitan entanglement available to any pair of users from both a single memory link and an intercity teleportation network.

add milestone after m5: "Two metropolitan-scale networks share entanglement through a repeater backbone longer than 500 km.". Reason: The European prototype defines a measurable backbone integration test between the intercity demonstrations and the continental target.
remove not found 2. Reason: The full DOE workshop report and the Nature article on teleportation between non-neighbouring nodes are accessible.
remove statement 1. Reason: RFC 9340 names support for distributed applications as an architectural goal without specifying a continental repeater network.
remove statement 0. Reason: The DOE explainer describes multi-hop networking in general, while the dated workshop report names the interstate repeater goal directly.
